question_en: Marcos Silva, CFA, and Clara Neves, CFA, are analysts at Alpha Capital, an independent research firm. Silva reads a blog post about Northwest Bank that details several fresh insights on company-specific growth. After doing his own thorough research on Northwest, Silva agrees with the blogger's analysis, although he expects this growth to take longer than the blogger predicts. Silva then writes a research report on Northwest and includes a restatement of the blogger's insights. Since he has changed some of the wording and the expected time horizon for growth, he does not reference the blog. Neves proofreads the report at Silva's request and agrees with his conclusion about the bank. With Silva's approval, Neves adds a chart from the US Federal Reserve, which is not copyrighted, that shows expected growth in bank reserves over the next year. She properly cites the US Federal Reserve as the source. According to the Code and Standards:
option_a: both Silva and Neves have violated the Standards.
option_b: Silva has violated the Standards, but Neves has not.
option_c: Neves has violated the Standards, but Silva has not.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities. In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation. Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." When a member or candidate becomes aware that violations of rules or laws are taking place, the Standard encourages the member or candidate first to report the situation to a supervisor or compliance department. If that is unsuccessful, members and candidates should then attempt to dissociate (ie, separate themselves) from the activity, not necessarily resign from the firm. Here, Villalba's most appropriate next step is to dissociate from the activity by requesting reassignment. She may need to resign if that request is not granted. Note that although the Standard strongly encourages reporting, it does not require the member or candidate to report unethical or illegal activities by others to government authorities or regulators (Choice A). (Choice C) Remaining in her current role is not an appropriate action. The Standard implies that by both continuing to associate with and failing to act on a legal violation, Villalba could be considered as taking part in or assisting with the illegal conduct.

question_en: Clem Benson, CFA, is the chief investment officer at Sterling Hospital. Sterling's board asks Benson for fundraising ideas. Benson suggests that if Sterling refers past contributors to him, he will conduct a personalized investment review for a fee of $1,000. In return, Benson will donate 50% of that fee to Sterling. After receiving board approval, Sterling promotes the fundraising campaign to its past contributors, informs them of Benson's arrangement, and refers 50 clients to Benson. The fundraiser raises $25,000 for Sterling. According to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, has Benson most likely violated the Standard?
option_b: Yes, since Benson receives income from the referrals.
option_c: Yes, since Benson receives the tax deduction for the donation instead of the contributors.
explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires members and candidates to avoid misleading investors (and potential investors) when communicating investment performance. The Standard applies to how performance is presented and measured. Although compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards® (GIPS) is recommended, a firm does not need to adopt GIPS to comply with this Standard. A firm must include both active and terminated accounts in its performance information. The information must clearly indicate when accounts were terminated. Failing to do so could mislead investors since the breakdown of returns for terminated accounts and active accounts cannot be easily determined. Firms must also indicate whether performance is calculated gross of (ie, before) or net of (ie, after) management fees. In this scenario, Statement 2 clearly states that performance data are gross of fees, so the materials comply with the Standard. Florenz Equities does not need to specify its management fees in its marketing materials (Choices B and C).

question_en: Maria Perez, CFA, is a portfolio manager for a small family office, Powell Investment Partners. Powell's investment policy does not allow managers to invest in individual hedge funds, but Perez gets approval to invest in funds of hedge funds. Perez decides to invest in Ashvale Group, a fund of hedge funds operated by a former colleague, Jose Rivera. She sees that Ashvale has posted strong returns in each of the past five years and remembers Rivera being highly diligent in his investment decisions when they worked together. Perez knows that fund-of-hedge-funds managers perform due diligence on each individual hedge fund in which they invest, so she feels comfortable with her decision. Has Perez violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?
option_b: No, since she worked with Rivera and is familiar with his work
option_c: No, since fund-of-hedge-funds managers do the due diligence on behalf of investors
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation concerns actions that may undermine investor trust in the integrity of the CFA profession and the financial markets. The Standard applies to all information presented to clients, colleagues, or the public. Misrepresentation can include: Omission: Presenting incomplete information or data in order to mislead Exaggeration: Inflating professional credentials or performance results Plagiarism: Quoting information without acknowledgment or citation In this scenario, Gerry Walsh has complied with the Standard by fully disclosing performance for the life of the account (Choice B). The Standard prohibits Members and Candidates from guaranteeing clients specific returns on investments since all investments carry some degree of risk. Although Walsh states that "similar long-term average returns are possible for others," he is not violating the Standard. Walsh is not promising such returns will be achieved, and he warns investors about "the potential for high volatility and significant losses." (Choice C) Walsh provides data conveying the risk of cryptocurrencies and advises they are not appropriate for all investors. The Standard is not violated since there is no omission of information that might result in investors being misled.

question_en: Morena Villalba, CFA, and Franco Aquirre, a Level I CFA candidate, both work in the private wealth department of a major bank and often work with the same clients. Villalba becomes aware that Aquirre receives compensation for each referral he makes to the bank's brokerage department that results in commissions but does not disclose that fact to clients. Also, she learns that Aquirre and a colleague have been able to hide the arrangement and fees from the firm. Villalba researches local law and believes that Aquirre's arrangement is illegal. She reports the situation to her supervisor, but after some time has passed, Villalba notices that Aquirre continues to benefit from his referrals, and she is not sure what to do next. According to Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which of the following actions is Villalba's most appropriate next step?
option_a: Resign from her employment at the bank
option_b: Request a transfer to another department of the bank
option_c: Remain in her role to document stronger evidence to present later
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to seek best price and best execution for client trades. "Best price" and "best execution" do not necessarily mean the lowest trading commission, but commissions paid to brokers to execute the trades must be commensurate with the value received. Soft dollar brokerage refers to the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to purchase investment services (eg, research). Since the client "pays" the commission out of client assets, these investment services are the property of the client, not the investment management firm, and must be used to benefit the client. Typically, brokers that offer value-added investment services charge higher commissions. Clients can choose not to have their accounts traded on a soft dollar basis if they do not feel the value is worth the cost. In this scenario, Johnson does not violate the Standard even though he directs all account trading to RMB. RMB reduced its commissions to match CCB's commissions; therefore, the clients that do not allow soft dollars are not paying extra to subsidize the research used by clients that allow soft dollars (Choice C). When RMB raises its prices, Johnson must switch accounts that do not allow soft dollars back to CCB. (Choice B) Johnson is not required to trade through only CCB despite them having the lowest commissions since RMB adds value to Pinnacle's clients through the research they offer, so long as the research is used to benefit Pinnacle's clients.

question_en:
Calvin Wurtz, CFA, is the founder and CEO of Florenz Equities, an asset management firm specializing in small-cap stocks. The firm's marketing materials display its average compounded returns over 5, 10, and 15 years. The materials include the following statements:

- Statement 1: "Average returns for each time period shown in these materials include returns from both currently active accounts and accounts that were terminated during that period."
- Statement 2: "We present average return data gross of management fees."

The materials do not specify the dates when accounts were terminated. The materials state that the firm does not comply with Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS).

Has Wurtz violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation with respect to Florenz's marketing materials?
option_b: Yes, only regarding average return data.
option_c: Yes, regarding both terminated accounts and average return data.
explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires members and candidates to avoid misleading investors (and potential investors) when communicating investment performance. The Standard applies to how performance is presented and measured. Although compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) is recommended, a firm does not need to adopt GIPS to comply with this Standard. A firm must include both active and terminated accounts in its performance information. The information must clearly indicate when accounts were terminated. Failing to do so could mislead investors since the breakdown of returns for terminated accounts and active accounts cannot be easily determined. Firms must also indicate whether performance is calculated gross of (ie, before) or net of (ie, after) management fees. In this scenario, Statement 2 clearly states that performance data are gross of fees, so the materials comply with the Standard. Florenz Equities does not need to specify its management fees in its marketing materials (Choices B and C). Things to remember: Standard III(D) requires members and candidates to present performance in a way that does not mislead investors. When presenting past performance in marketing materials, firms should include returns from both terminated and active accounts and state when accounts were terminated. Firms must also indicate whether returns are gross or net of fees, but there is no requirement to disclose the fees in marketing materials.

question_en: Gerry Walsh, CFA, trades only cryptocurrencies through an account at Mayday Securities. Since the account was opened in January 20X7, Walsh has earned an average monthly return of 3.5%. However, returns have been very volatile, and the monthly gains and losses often exceed 10%. In January 20X8, Walsh starts a subscriber-based online investment newsletter providing information on his experience with cryptocurrencies and monthly returns. In the newsletter, Walsh suggests similar long-term average returns are possible for others if they follow his strategies. He states that cryptocurrency trading can generate large gains, but adds that it carries the potential for high volatility and significant losses. Although Walsh wants more subscribers, he fully discloses the account's performance in 20X7 and notes that cryptocurrency investments may not be appropriate for all investors. Based on the actions described, does Walsh violate Standard I(C) Misrepresentation by issuing the newsletter?
option_b: Yes, since he presents performance for only 20X7.
option_c: Yes, since he knows cryptocurrencies are not appropriate for all subscribers.
explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) permits only CFA Institute members who have earned the CFA designation to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders. Wijngaards' guilty plea and the subsequent revocation of her charter mean that she forfeited her right to use the designation. However, as interpreted by CFA Institute, Standard VII(B) does allow former charterholders to state that they previously held the designation. Nothing in the Code or Standards requires former charterholders to apply for reinstatement as a condition of stating that they are former charterholders (Choice B). Furthermore, the Standards do not prohibit statements of objective fact. Wijngaards can verify that she once held the CFA designation. So long as Wijngaards's statement does not lead others to conclude that she expects to be reinstated, the Standards do not prevent her from stating that she previously was a charterholder (Choice C).

question_en: Matt Fabiano, CFA, is the senior portfolio manager at Marco Investment Advisors (MIA). All of MIA's clients gave Fabiano discretion over their accounts and, as part of his service, he directs trades to a number of brokerage firms. Fabiano discovers that if he trades exclusively with Strollo Brokerage Inc. (SB), MIA could participate in SB's client referral program, allowing MIA to serve more clients. Based on MIA's analysis, Fabiano concludes that clients are neither harmed by nor benefit from using SB as a broker. With respect to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, if Fabiano trades exclusively with SB, most likely he:
option_a: does not violate the Standard since he has discretion.
option_b: violates the Standard since clients do not receive a benefit.
option_c: does not violate the Standard since he does not receive a benefit.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from trading on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information. However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form investment conclusions. This research approach is referred to as the mosaic theory, and it recognizes that analysts form conclusions from various sources of information. Conclusions formed through the mosaic process, even when based on information that would be considered material and nonpublic if it came directly from a reliable source (eg, the company), do not violate the Standard. In this scenario, Eric Saul used public information, including social media posts, industry publications, and financial statements. His discussion at Gamma Company, although nonpublic, is not material since the senior vice president simply confirmed Saul's market research and indicated nothing about Gamma's intentions (Choice C). (Choice B) Saul's purchase of Gamma did not violate the Standard since he did not use material nonpublic information to reach his conclusion regarding Gamma. He also treated Skye's clients in an equitable manner by purchasing the stock for all suitable client portfolios.

question_en: Hudson Bright, CFA, just received his certificate in quantitative finance. As part of his studies, he developed training modules for financial modeling. Soon after receiving his certificate, Bright joins QED Consulting, a quantitative analysis consulting firm, and posts news about his certificate and new job on social media. The local CFA Society president sees his post and asks him to teach financial modeling classes. After determining that the time commitment will not hinder his performance at QED, Bright agrees to teach a monthly, one-hour class for 6 months at €500 per class. He advises QED of his plans in an email that states, "I am writing to inform you that I have agreed to partner with the local CFA Society to teach financial modeling classes. Please contact me with any questions." He does not receive a response and begins teaching the classes. Has Bright most likely violated Standard IV(A) Loyalty to Employer?
option_b: Yes, since he started teaching prior to receiving approval from QED.
option_c: Yes, since his notice to QED left out required information on compensation and duration.
explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, they must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the portfolio." Standard III(C) Suitability prescribes how the manager must act when investing on behalf of the client. Suitability entails evaluating whether an investment's expected risk and return match the client's risk tolerance and return objectives. Suitability cannot determine until the manager knows the client's investment objectives and constraints. (Choice A) Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis states that managers must diligently exercise thoroughness when taking investment actions. Given Smith's expertise with the Conservative Portfolio, it is reasonable to assume that the violation does not involve a lack of diligence. (Choice C) The Conservative Portfolio has more risk than a cash portfolio since it has exposure to equities and emerging markets. There is no prudent investor test to determine whether the portfolio is appropriate or not. No matter how "temporary" the investment is intended to be, it does not excuse Smith from first assessing whether the investment is suitable for the client's risk and return objectives.

question_en: Trevor Johnson, CFA, joins Pinnacle Advisors as an equity trader. Pinnacle uses Research Market Brokers (RMB) for all trades from accounts that allow soft dollar arrangements and Cost Cutter Brokers (CCB) for those that do not. RMB does not have the lowest execution price but offers research used for the benefit of Pinnacle's clients. CCB offers the lowest price execution available for Pinnacle. After a slow trading month, Pinnacle is below its soft dollar trading commitment to RMB. RMB offers to temporarily lower the price of its trades to match CCB until the commitment is reached as long as all trades, including those on accounts that do not allow soft dollar arrangements, are made through their brokerage. Based on the Code and Standards, Johnson:
option_a: can temporarily trade all accounts through RMB since it lowered its price.
option_b: can only trade stocks through CCB for all accounts since it is usually the lowest-priced.
option_c: cannot use trades for accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements to meet the
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation requires Members and Candidates to avoid any practices that deceive market participants through the distortion of securities prices or trading volume. Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing misleading information) and transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The Standard is not meant to prevent the use of legitimate strategies that limit a trade's impact on the market when trading large positions or low- liquidity stocks. The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is whether the trading strategy is intended to deceive market participants. If the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard. In this scenario, Annika Goncharov uses a legitimate strategy of breaking up a large position of a low-liquidity stock to limit the impact of the sale on the price. Annika's strategy has not violated the Standard (Choice B). Boris Goncharov intends to distort market prices by making market participants believe there are more buyers of Bright Sky Capital's stock than there are. Since market participants cannot see that Boris is driving both the buying and the selling activity, the trading is deceptive and has violated the Standard (Choice C).

question_en: Shweta Reddy, CFA, proctors the last day of the Level III CFA exam. While conducting a walkthrough during the exam, she sees one Candidate glancing at another Candidate's monitor. She notices that the question on the cheating Candidate's screen is about the portfolio management of pension funds. After the exam, Shweta joins the other proctors for drinks at a local bar and runs into an old friend, a doctor who has no plans to take any CFA exam. While chatting with the doctor, she mentions her proctoring experience and says, "I caught someone blatantly cheating on a pension fund question. He wasn't even trying to hide it!" Has Reddy most likely violated Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs?
option_b: No, since the last day of exams has been completed.
option_c: No, since she did not provide specific details about the question.
explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." To comply with Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Members and Candidates must use credible return data when preparing performance information for current or potential clients. Clients must receive performance information that is free from distorted data that may be misleading. To comply with the Standard, Members and Candidates need to fully disclose exceptions and avoid any disclosures that may misrepresent performance. Shepherd accurately portrays her work with the Green Fund and does not mislead her clients, who are made aware that she worked for the Green Fund from 20X6 to 20X8. (Choice B) Shepherd does not violate the Standard by reporting the Green Fund's performance gross of fees since she discloses its fee schedule. (Choice C) An advisor must report an account's returns even if the advisor is no longer associated with that account. Otherwise, the advisor might conceal accounts that performed poorly, leading to the advisor's termination.

question_en: Five years ago, Marlijn Wijngaards pled guilty to a finance-related felony. She had previously earned the CFA designation, but her charter was revoked as a result of the plea. Wijngaards has applied to CFA Institute to reinstate her charter and membership. Her application is pending. In her résumé, Wijngaards refers to herself as a "Former CFA Charterholder." Does this reference violate Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
option_b: Yes, since she cannot refer to the CFA designation unless her application is successful.
option_c: Yes, since the revocation prohibits her from indicating that she ever held the designation.
explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, they must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the portfolio." Standard III(C) Suitability addresses Members' and Candidates' responsibilities to assess the suitability of investments for each client. Members and Candidates that manage a pooled investment vehicle to a specific investment mandate have a responsibility to ensure the suitability of investments for the fund, specifically making sure investments adhere to the mandate. Members and Candidates cannot be expected to ensure suitability for every investor in the fund; that is the responsibility of the investor or investor's advisor. In this instance, Stephanie Williams is an institutional portfolio manager, so her duty is to ensure suitability to the fund's mandate. Since she is not in an advisory relationship with Jeffrey Jones, or any investor, she is not responsible for assessing the suitability of the fund for his investment portfolio (Choices B and C). Therefore, Williams did not violate the Standard.

A few weeks later, Gamma announces a new line of herbal rose tea. Did Saul most likely violate Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?

explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from engaging in behavior that undermines the integrity of CFA Institute, its programs, and the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter. To uphold the integrity of the charter, the CFA Institute takes care to ensure that confidential information about exams is not shared by anyone. For Members and Candidates, sharing such information is a violation of the Standard. Members may not disclose: questions that are set to appear on the exam or are under consideration, any parts of the deliberation process related to the exam, or information related to the grading of questions. Graders may not share information with anyone outside of the development or grading process. Since Han is not part of the grading process, Yoo may not discuss any information relating to the grading of questions, whether it is specific details or general information. By doing so, she violates the Standard. If this information were shared with other participants in the grading process, it would not violate the Standard. (Choices A and C) Han does not violate the Standard since he is not part of the exam's development, administering, or grading process and therefore does not know any information to disclose. His only source of information is a social media post.

explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires members and candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when investing. It is not uncommon for a member or candidate to transact in the same investments as a client or even alongside the client. This situation does not violate the Standard provided that: the client is not disadvantaged by the trade, the member or candidate does not benefit from the client transactions, and the member or candidate adheres to all applicable regulatory requirements. Likewise, a manager has no obligation to invest personal funds in the same strategy as clients do since the manager may have different risk and return objectives and different constraints (eg, liquidity needs) than the clients. In this scenario, Ivanov complied with the Standard. Ivanov has no specific obligation to inform clients of his personal transactions (Choice B). His sale ran counter to the long-term advice given to clients, but since he did not violate the guidelines above, no infringement occurred (Choice C).

question_en: Annika and Boris Goncharov are siblings, CFA charterholders, and investors of Bright Sky Capital (BSC). Annika and Boris hold more than RUB 100 million each in BSC stock, and each plans to sell 10% to diversify their separate portfolios. However, BSC is a lightly traded stock, and the siblings agree that large sales would likely cause the company's stock price to decline. Annika decides to break up her sales into small batches of limit orders and sell them over multiple days to minimize the impact on the stock's price. Still, Annika's sales cause BSC's stock price to decline. Boris similarly decides to sell his holdings in batches, but he simultaneously purchases half the amount he sells to ensure the stock price is unaffected by his trades. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is most likely violated by:
option_b: both Boris and Annika.
option_c: neither Boris nor Annika.
explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires Members and Candidates to provide a fair, accurate, and complete record of their performance. To avoid misrepresentation, a manager, firm, portfolio, or composite must provide full disclosure of all aspects of performance to all clients, prospective clients, and prospective employers. If the details are fully disclosed, the Standard allows the presentation of performance information from prior employers, accounts managed by multiple people, and simulations. Performance data from a prior employer cannot be used without written permission from the employer. In this scenario, Erik Johansen receives written approval from his prior employer, Henderson Bank, before presenting data on the returns he achieved there as a portfolio manager. The marketing brochure fully discloses both this background and the fact that Claire Olsen's model returns are simulated, so the Standard is not being violated (Choices B and C).

question_en: Stephanie Williams, CFA, is the portfolio manager of the Lantern Latin American Equity Fund (LLAEF). LLAEF is a mutual fund that invests exclusively in stocks listed in Central and South America. While attending her daughter's gymnastics practice, Williams discusses LLAEF with Jeffrey Jones, who also has a daughter in the class. Jones states that he is a conservative investor, investing primarily in a balanced fund, and has never considered investing in Latin American equities before. Williams gives a very optimistic assessment of the economic conditions in the region and states that Latin American equities are among the most undervalued globally. Williams says, "I believe Latin America is likely to be the best performing emerging market region in the world over the next few years. This fund is a 'no brainer' and adds great diversification benefits to any portfolio." Has Williams most likely violated Standard III(C) Suitability?
option_b: Yes, as Williams recommended a portfolio allocation
option_c: Yes, as Williams recommended a specific investment
explanation_en: Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires Members and Candidates to place clients' interests ahead of their own. The Standard mandates that, for a given security, the firm's or employee's trades must be placed after client trades. There is no specific waiting period, but firms must give clients a reasonable amount of time to act on recommendations. Sidney Fletcher violated the Standard by trading Responsive Market Tech, Inc. for the firm's account before PPG Investments' clients had time to act upon Kathy Harriet's advice. Fletcher should have postponed trading until clients could reasonably have acted on Harriet's recommendation. (Choice B) The resulting price after Fletcher's trade does not mitigate his violation. Fletcher is not exempted from violating the Standard just for having no price impact. (Choice C) Harriet complied by delivering the meeting transcript and her recommendation as soon as possible, but Fletcher should have placed the firm's trades after clients could reasonably be expected to receive and use the recommendation.

question_en: Soomin Yoo, CFA, is helping grade the most recent Level 3 exam. At dinner one evening, she discusses the grading process with a friend, Minsoo Han, CFA, who is not participating in the grading process. Yoo states "I'm surprised how many people are missing the question on fixed income investing strategies. It didn't come across to me as that difficult." Han responds "If that's the case, candidates might be in trouble. I read on a social media post that the multiple-choice section also had more fixed income questions than in other recent exams." According to the Standards, is it most likely that:
option_a: both Yoo and Han have violated the Standards.
option_b: Yoo has violated the Standards but Han has not.
option_c: Han has violated the Standards but Yoo has not.
explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that this information is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires Members and Candidates to provide a fair, accurate, and complete performance record. Misrepresenting performance is a violation of the Standard, whether it is in the measurement or presentation. Providing a complete performance record entails including all pertinent portfolios or composites when calculating the performance of a firm. Rahul Agarwal violates the Standard by excluding terminated portfolios from the firm's performance and not making any note that they were excluded (Choice A). By excluding terminated portfolios, Agarwal misrepresents Bagh Capital's performance and fails to provide the prospective clients with an accurate and complete picture of historical returns. (Choice C) Distributing a summary of performance is allowed under the Standard. Best practices call for summaries to include a note about the limited nature of the presentation.

question_en: Vladimir Ivanov, CFA, is the portfolio manager of a separately managed account (SMA) that invests equally in 20 different large-cap international value stocks. Most of Ivanov's personal investments are invested in the same strategy. Since Ivanov's twin daughters are enrolling in college this year, he needs to sell a portion of his holdings to pay for their tuition. To generate a tax loss, Ivanov sells the entire position of one holding instead of selling equal portions of all 20 positions in his account. According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, did Ivanov most likely comply with the Standard?
option_b: No, by not informing his clients before the trade
option_c: No, by entirely divesting from a holding that is still held in client accounts
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities. In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation. Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires members and candidates to understand local laws. When members or candidates do business in more than one country, they are required to know and understand both the Standards of Professional Conduct and the laws and regulations of each country. In all professional activities, they must follow the strictest of the applicable rules. Telluci does business in both Country Y (where Bull Advisors is based) and Country X (where the new client resides). Before doing business with the client, Telluci must be familiar with the set of securities laws and regulations in Country X—in addition to those of Country Y and the Code and Standards—so that he knows which rules to apply if a conflict arises. Without this knowledge, Telluci could not make an informed judgment. (Choices B and C) Although the rules of Country X are less strict than those of Country Y or the Code and Standards, Telluci violated Standard I(A) by not familiarizing himself with and understanding all the applicable laws and regulations.

question_en: Erik Johansen, CFA, and Claire Olsen, CFA, decide to start their own fund. They create a marketing brochure that includes the following: ● "Claire Olsen, CFA, a self-employed investor, has developed a proprietary model focused on growth stocks. The model achieved a simulated annualized return of 15% over the past five years." ● "Erik Johansen, CFA, averaged a 12% annual return from 20X1 to 20X7 while working as a portfolio manager at his prior employer, Henderson Bank." Johansen received written approval from Henderson to use the return data. Based on this information, have Johansen and Olsen most likely violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation?
option_b: Yes, by using Johansen's return data from a prior employer.
option_c: Yes, by using the simulated returns of Olsen's model and not the actual performance history.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' best interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to seek best price and best execution for client trades. "Best price" and "best execution" do not necessarily mean the lowest trading commission, but commissions must be commensurate with the value received. Examples of sell-side factors to consider for best price and execution include: Idea generation Research and analysis Overall execution price Commission paid Charterholders must be especially diligent in applying best price and execution standards when there are soft dollar arrangements. Soft dollar brokerage is the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to pay for investment research. Such research is considered an asset of the client, not the manager, and must be used to benefit the client. In this instance, Sarah Cohen should have directed the large order of thinly traded small-cap stock to the firm that could best execute the trade, which is SCSI. She violated the Standard by failing to obtain best price and best execution for the express purpose of satisfying the firm's soft dollar commitment and not for the client's benefit. (Choice A) Soft dollar brokerage is not prohibited by the Standards, but the manager has a duty of loyalty to use this asset for the exclusive benefit of the client. (Choice C) Directing trading activity to firms that provide decision-making value to the manager is not prohibited by the Standards.

question_en: Aline Costa, CFA, is a financial advisor for Solar Bank. At a conference, Costa meets Juanita Carvalho, a portfolio manager for Lunar Financial. Carvalho tells Costa about a propriety quantitative model developed by Lunar that aims to predict interest rate changes. Costa reads Lunar's sales literature on the model to understand how it works, its assumptions, and its testing parameters, which included both extreme positive and negative scenarios. Of the following, Costa can most appropriately begin integrating the model into her research process:
option_b: after thoroughly testing the model herself.
option_c: after taking the time to learn the technical aspects of the model.
explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements allows additional compensation agreements with third parties, including clients. However, Members and Candidates must disclose such agreements in full and obtain written permission from all parties involved before accepting compensation that could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with their employers. Gifts, benefits, and other compensation do not need to be monetary to require approval. In this scenario, Dimitri Federov's actions violate the Standard in both arrangements. His options compensation agreement with Safe Bank must be disclosed to Arrow Financial in full before he accepts it. The fact that he has not recommended Safe's trust services to his clients and has not received any options does not excuse him from disclosing the arrangement to Arrow, as it could create a conflict of interest later (Choice A). Likewise, his compensation agreement with Natasha Popova must be approved in writing by Arrow before he accepts it since the Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary compensation (Choice B).
